1.title: Getting to know you
1.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

The main text of the lesson.

Before you read: two strangers sit in a room and ask each other 36 personal questions for 45 minutes.

Do you think they feel closer afterwards? Decide first, then read and find out if you were right.

There is no right answer here. This is your prediction.

Three sets of questions

In 1997 an American psychologist called Arthur Aron tried an experiment. He put two strangers in a room and gave them a list of thirty-six questions. They had forty-five minutes. The questions came in three sets, and each set was more personal than the last. The first set was easy: Who is your dream dinner guest? The last set was not: When did you last cry in front of another person?

Another group of strangers got small talk instead — the weather, work, family, favourite food. What did you do at the weekend? Do you like this weather?

Aron’s team then recorded how close each pair felt. The result surprised everyone. The pairs who asked the thirty-six questions felt much closer than the small-talk pairs, and many of them said they felt as close to this stranger as they did in their closest relationships. One pair from that first experiment later got married.

Twenty-five years later, other researchers asked more than 1,800 people to have one shallow conversation and one deep one. Before they started, most people expected to prefer the small talk. Afterwards, most people preferred the deep conversation.

So why do we still chat about the weather? Partly because we are busy. But mostly because we are wrong: we think other people are not interested in our real answers.

You can still find the thirty-six questions online, and people share them in posts and send them to friends by text every year. The researchers were careful, though. Nobody made a promise that strangers would become friends. The questions worked in a laboratory, with two people who had agreed to take part and who both knew the rules.

Sources. Aron, Melinat, Aron, Vallone & Bator (1997), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 23(4) · Kardas, Kumar & Epley (2022), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Text written for this course.

2.title: A day in three lives
2.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Three people, the same twenty-four hours.

Before you read: a night nurse, a freelancer and a farmer.

Who do you think sleeps least? Choose one, then read and find out whether you were right.

No right answer yet. This is your prediction.

The average day — and three people who don’t have one

Every year the American government asks thousands of people one question: what did you do yesterday, hour by hour? The answers become the American Time Use Survey — an average day that almost nobody lives.

A full-time worker works 8.4 hours on a weekday and 5.6 hours at the weekend. Eighty per cent of employed people work on a weekday, but only thirty per cent work at the weekend. They sleep about nine hours and spend nearly five on leisure, half of it television.

That is the average. Here are three people nowhere near it.

Aliya is a night nurse. Her shift runs from seven in the evening to seven in the morning. She hardly ever eats a proper meal at work, and she rarely sleeps well: nurses sleep about eighty-three minutes less before a shift. On her days off she stays in, does the housework, helps her son with his homework and goes swimming twice a week.

Dias is a freelancer. A third of employed people now work from home; Dias does it every day. He writes a to-do list each morning and works indoors until dark. He often works late. He never goes to the gym and gave up running years ago, but he plays chess online twice a week.

Ruslan is a farmer. He gets up early, always, even in winter, and spends the day outdoors. His work is his exercise. In summer he hardly ever has a free weekend, but every October he goes camping.

The survey gives you a number. It does not give you a day. Ask any of the three of them what a normal week looks like, and all three will tell you theirs is completely ordinary.

Sources. All national figures: American Time Use Survey 2024, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — a work of the U.S. federal government and therefore in the public domain. Nurses’ sleep: Witkoski Stimpfel et al., NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing. The three portraits are written for this course to illustrate the data.

After reading

5.title: The things in our homes
5.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

A house where the writer cannot name anything.

Before you read: the writer is looking after a stranger’s house for a month.

What do you think will be hardest about it?

A prediction, not an answer.

The house where I’m staying

I’m house-sitting for a friend of a friend this month. I’ve never met the owners — they’re the people who put an advert on a house-swap website, and I answered it.

The house is beautiful and completely strange to me. In the kitchen there’s a machine which washes the dishes, but I can’t find the button that starts it. There’s no proper cooker either, only the box that heats food in two minutes. I love cooking, so that is the thing which disappoints me most.

The bathroom is the room where everything confuses me. The bowl you wash your hands in looks like a sheet of paper, and on the first morning I couldn’t work the metal thing the water comes out of. There are candles everywhere, and towels so soft that I am almost afraid to use them.

In the bedroom there is nowhere to put my clothes — no tall cupboard where you hang things, and no low one with drawers either. There are white rugs on every floor, which is a problem for someone who spills things.

Outside, on the wall, there’s a big round dish that points at the sky, and a small camera which watches the front door. My friend says the owners collect old maps, and that the frames in the hall are worth more than my car. I am being very careful.

I’m enjoying it. But I still miss my own bed, my own duvet, and a kitchen where I know what everything is called.

Source note. Written for this course. The situation and the objects come from the house-sitting accounts in the Navigate B1 Unit 2 recordings.

7.title: The man who fell to earth
7.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Two texts. The story from the ground, and what happened two years later.

Before you read: look at the picture and the title of Text A.

What do you think worried the ground team most? Choose one, then read and find out.

A prediction, not an answer.

Text A — The day I watched a man fall from the sky

I worked for the ground team at Roswell, New Mexico, on 14 October 2012. My job was small — I checked the radios — but I remember every minute.

We waited two weeks for the wind. On an earlier date in October the weather stopped us an hour before launch. Then, on the fourteenth, the desert was still.

At sunrise the balloon went up, enormous, with plastic thinner than a shopping bag. Inside the capsule sat Felix Baumgartner, the Austrian pilot who wanted to jump from the edge of space. The balloon lifted him for two and a half hours, up to almost 39 kilometres.

Then he opened the door and moved forwards onto the step. Nobody spoke. On my screen I saw the curve of the Earth behind him.

He jumped at 5.37 p.m.

For the first half-minute everything looked perfect. He fell towards the desert faster and faster and passed the speed of sound — the first person in history to do that outside an aircraft. Then he started to turn. He went round and round, and we could not stop him. The engineer next to me said nothing. I did not breathe.

Baumgartner pulled out of the spin himself: he pushed his arms backwards and dropped his head. Four minutes and nineteen seconds after he left the capsule, his parachute opened.

He landed on his feet in the desert, and then he fell onto his knees. The rescue team reached him in ninety seconds.

People always ask me the same question: did he know he was in danger? He knew. He climbed into that capsule anyway.

1 · Read Text A once. Answer the two questions.
1What is the writer’s main point?
2Which title suits Text A best?
2 · Read again. True or false?
1The writer was inside the capsule.
2Bad weather stopped an earlier attempt.
3The balloon took more than two hours to go up.
4The spin started immediately after he jumped.
5The ground team stopped the spin from their desks.
6He fell for less than five minutes before the parachute opened.
7He fell over after he landed.
3 · Put the six events in the order they happened in Text A.
4 · Find the word in Text A that means…
1very, very big →
2the line where the Earth seems to bend → the
3to arrive at someone or something →
4to take air in and out of your body →
5completely quiet and not moving →
5 · Now read Text B.

Text B — Two years later, in the same desert

Two years after Baumgartner, a second man went up from the same corner of New Mexico — and almost nobody knew about it.

Alan Eustace was 57, an engineer, and a senior manager at Google. He paid for the project himself. He did not use a capsule at all. He simply hung underneath a helium balloon in a special suit, with a parachute on his back.

On 24 October 2014 the balloon lifted him for two and a half hours, up to 41,419 metres — about two and a half kilometres higher than Baumgartner. Then he cut himself loose. Ninety seconds later he passed the speed of sound. He opened his parachute at about 5,500 metres and landed in the desert fifteen minutes after he left the balloon.

Baumgartner’s team invited the world’s media. Eustace invited one journalist. His altitude record still stands today, and his suit is now in a museum in Washington.

Source note. Text A is written for this course: the events, dates and figures are from the public record of the Red Bull Stratos mission of 14 October 2012, and the narrator is invented to tell the story from the ground — no words are attributed to anyone who took part. Text B is an educational adaptation of reporting by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale, the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum and NPR on the StratEx jump of 24 October 2014.

6 · Text A, Text B, or both? Choose for each sentence.
1The man travelled up inside a capsule.
2The jump started near Roswell, New Mexico.
3The team kept the project quiet until it was over.
4The man went faster than the speed of sound.
5The man paid for the project himself.
6The balloon took about two and a half hours to go up.
7This man still holds the altitude record.
7 · The texts do not say this directly. What is the best answer?
1Why does the writer of Text A mention the engineer’s hands on the desk?
2Why did Eustace invite only one journalist?
3Which sentence best describes the difference between the two projects?
Write it down

Read your answer back. Every verb about 2012 or 2014 should be in the Past Simple. Then mark this done.

10.title: Changing direction
10.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Three people who started again, and none of them planned to.

Before you read: at what age is it too late to change career completely?

Choose one. Then read and see whether the text agrees with you.

No right answer yet. This is your opinion.

Three people who started again

Most people decide on a career in their twenties and stop thinking about it. These three did the opposite.

Nadia was a lawyer for eleven years. She was good at it, but she hated going to the office. At thirty-four she left home for the first time in her life, moved to another city and started training to become a nurse. “I didn’t want to spend another decade doing something I disliked,” she says. She finished her training in her late thirties and now works nights in a children’s hospital. She has never regretted leaving law.

Tomas took up the guitar when he was a teenager. He kept playing all through university, but he chose to study engineering because it seemed safer. He worked as an engineer until he was forty-two. Then his company closed. Instead of looking for another job, he decided to teach music. He now performs in a small concert hall twice a month and enjoys teaching more than he expected.

Grace is the oldest of the three. She retired at sixty-one and immediately got bored. She avoided telling her family, but she missed working. So, in her sixties, she began studying again — and last year she qualified as a conductor. She hopes to lead a full orchestra before she is seventy.

None of them planned to change direction. All three would do it again.

Their advice is similar. Expect to feel foolish for about a year. Avoid asking people who have never changed anything. And do not give up doing something you love just because somebody tells you it is not a real job.

Note. Written for this course as a reading text. Nadia, Tomas and Grace are invented, and no words are attributed to a real person.

13.title: Your world in objects
13.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Five things, one person

The five objects somebody chose, and the reason none of them cost much.

Before you read: a museum asks you to choose five objects from your home that would tell a stranger who you are. Which of these would you look for first?

A prediction, not an answer. Read and see what the writer chose.

Five things, one person

A museum in my city asked people to do something strange: choose five objects from your home that would tell a stranger who you are. Not the most valuable five. The five that mean something. I thought it would take ten minutes. It took me a week.

The first was easy. A green bicycle. Not the green bicycle in the photograph on my wall — that one was stolen — but the plastic-and-metal one I bought to replace it. It is not fashionable and it is certainly not brand new. The condition is terrible. I have ridden it every day for nine years.

Then a leather notebook, heavy, with thin paper and a pale blue cover. I do not write in it. I collect train tickets in it, and the collection is now nearly full.

Then an antique wooden spoon that belonged to my grandmother. It is the only object in the house that is older than my father.

The fourth was a lamp — a shiny, bright, completely useless lamp that a friend gave me. My flat is minimalist because I cannot afford furniture, and the lamp is the one thing in it that argues with the walls.

The fifth took the rest of the week. In the end I chose a key. It opens a door in a city I no longer live in, and it is not suitable for anything now, but I have never been able to throw it away.

Here is what surprised me. Nothing on my list was expensive, and nothing was essential. Ask somebody what possessions they own and they will tell you about money. Ask them for five objects and they will tell you about their life.

Note. Written for this course as a reading text, in the first person. The museum project and the writer are invented; the idea — a personal collection chosen for meaning rather than value — is the one behind the time-capsule and ‘object stories’ projects that museums run. No words are attributed to a real person.

14.title: It’s all about the money
14.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Three ways to be wrong about money

The main text of the lesson.

Before you read. Three people are described. What do you think they have in common?

Three ways to be wrong about money

Ask three people how they manage their money and you will get three different answers — and all three will tell you they are doing it right.

Aizhan is a saver. She transfers a little money into a savings account every month, she never has any debt, and she checks her balance almost every day. She has enough for an emergency. But she also says no to almost everything: a few dinners with friends a year, no holidays, no small treats. Her sister says she saves too much and lives too little.

Timur is the opposite. He earns a good salary, but there isn’t much left at the end of the month. He can’t tell you where it goes — a coffee here, a taxi there. He has a credit card, and now he owes the bank a lot of money. Every year he promises to pay it back. Every year he doesn’t.

Then there is Marat, who is careful with big things and careless with small ones. He spent months choosing a cheap flat, and he pays a low rent. But he wastes money on things he forgets: three streaming services he never watches, a gym with a monthly fee he has used twice, a jacket he never sent back for a refund.

You can measure a salary. You cannot easily measure the money that leaves quietly, in small amounts, without a decision — and no statistic on Timur’s bank app will tell him where it went.

Most of us are one of these three. The interesting question is not how much you earn. It is how many decisions you make without noticing — and whether there is enough left when you finally do.

Note. Written for this course as a reading text. Aizhan, Timur and Marat are invented, and no words are attributed to a real person. The text makes no statistical claim and quotes no survey.

16.title: The quiet ones
16.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

The quiet ones

The main text of the lesson.

Before you read. Look at the title. Who do you think “the quiet ones” are?

The quiet ones

Some people love a big group. They talk to everyone, they share their ideas quickly, and they feel happy when the room is looking at them. We call these people extroverts. Other people are different. They think first and speak later, they prefer a small group or an empty room, and they often do their best work alone. These are introverts — the quiet ones.

For a long time, most schools and most companies wanted the first type. A confident, sociable student got more attention than a shy one. In many offices the loudest voice in the meeting was also the most powerful voice. But is that fair?

The writer Susan Cain says no. Her best-selling book Quiet argues that introverts are just as creative and just as hard-working as extroverts. They are usually more patient, too, and they are often better listeners. Their ideas are not louder. They are simply slower — and sometimes they are the strongest ideas in the room.

Cain says something more surprising as well: a team of only extroverts is not the best team. A good team needs both. The talkers move a project forward; the quiet ones notice the problem nobody mentioned.

Of course, nobody is one hundred per cent one type. Most of us are a bit of both, and we change with the situation. The important thing is not to become somebody else. If you are the quietest person in your class, that is not a weakness. It is a different kind of strength.

Sources. Written for this course. The argument it summarises — that introverts are undervalued in schools and offices, and that mixed teams work better — is from Susan Cain, Quiet (2012). No wording is taken from the book.

19.title: The future of getting around
19.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

What has already changed, and what the experts are ready to promise.

Before you read: which of these do you think will be normal in your city in twenty years?

Choose two. Then read and see whether the text agrees with you.

No right answer yet. This is your prediction.

Getting around in 2045

Nobody can predict the future perfectly. But look at what has already happened, and some of it becomes easier to guess.

In the last twenty years the picture has changed fast. Shenzhen, a Chinese city of twelve million people, replaced every diesel bus with an electric one and cut its fuel use sharply. Paris has built hundreds of kilometres of new cycle lanes. Dozens of countries have opened high-speed lines, and a journey that once took a whole day now takes three hours.

So what will happen next? Experts are confident about some of it. Cities will get quieter, because electric engines make almost no noise. The air will get cleaner: there will be less pollution from petrol and diesel. Public transport will become more efficient — buses will arrive when the app says they will, and one bus pass will work on every service in the city. Fares might go up, though. Clean transport is not cheap.

Other things are far less certain. Cars might disappear from city centres completely — or they might not. Some people think we will all travel in driverless taxis; others are not so sure. Flying taxis might work for short journeys between airports, but they probably won’t replace the train.

One prediction is safe. Traffic jams won’t disappear by themselves. If a city wants greener streets, it has to build the cycle lanes and the tracks first. The technology is the easy part.

And the people who live far from any main road? In small towns the bus is often the only service, and it is not always reliable. New developments — electric minibuses you order on your phone — might finally make village transport convenient.

22.title: The amazing human brain
22.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

What the brain really does, and what people only think it does.

Before you read: many people say we use only ten per cent of the brain.

Do you think that is true? Decide first, then read and find out if you were right.

There is no right answer yet. This is your prediction.

What the brain can really do

People love stories about the brain. One of them says that we use only ten per cent of it. It is a myth. Scientists can now watch the brain at work, and nobody has ever found a silent ninety per cent. The brain is about two per cent of your body, but it takes about twenty per cent of your energy.

Other myths are just as popular. In the 1990s many people believed that classical music could make a child more intelligent. Researchers checked it carefully. Music can put you in a better mood, and a good mood helps you solve problems — but Mozart cannot give a child a talent it did not have.

So what is really true? In 2000 a team in London studied taxi drivers. To get their licence, the drivers had to learn every street in the city. The part of the brain we use for map reading was larger in the drivers than in other people, and the longer they had driven, the larger it was. They were not born with this ability. They built it.

That is the interesting part. Ten years ago you could not understand this sentence. Now you can read it. Nothing changed in your head by accident: you practised, and the connections grew.

The brain can also do something no machine can: it can imagine a place it has never seen. Computers are still not able to copy that — and they are not able to feel emotions either.

Your brain will not be able to give you a perfect memory: it cannot remember everything you read, and it never could. But almost everyone can achieve something new — a language, an instrument, a different job — at almost any age.

Sources. Ten-per-cent myth and brain energy use: Society for Neuroscience, Brain Facts; Raichle & Gusnard (2002), PNAS · Mozart effect: Pietschnig, Voracek & Formann (2010), Intelligence · London taxi drivers: Maguire et al. (2000), PNAS. Text written for this course.

23.title: The rules of school
23.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

One country took most of the rules away. Then it kept one.

Before you read: one country has almost no school exams before the age of eighteen.

What do you think happened to its results? Decide first, then read and find out.

There is no right answer yet. This is your prediction.

The country that took the rules away

In most school systems the rules are easy to see. You have to wear a uniform. You must be in your seat when the bell rings. You have to pass an entrance exam to get into a good school, and you have to sit tests every year to prove that you deserve your grade.

Finland decided to try something else. Finnish children do not start school until they are seven. They don’t have to take a single national exam until they are about eighteen. Nearly every child goes to a state school, and the few private schools that exist are not allowed to charge fees, so parents cannot buy a better education. Homework is light. The school day is short.

But one rule in Finland is very strict. To stand in front of a class, a teacher must have a master’s degree, and the courses that train them are harder to get into than law or medicine. A Finnish teacher doesn’t have to follow a national plan hour by hour — they can choose how to teach their own subject — because the system trusts a qualification it made difficult to get.

Its success surprised everybody. For twenty years Finland has been near the top of the international tests in reading, maths and science, with less testing than almost anyone else.

Nobody says the country is perfect, and its results have fallen a little since 2006. Copying it is not simple either: a system that trusts its teachers has to build that trust first, and that takes a generation. But the lesson is not that rules are bad. It is that a system has to decide where the rules belong — in the classroom, or in the choice of the person standing in it.

Sources. Finnish National Agency for Education, Education system · OECD PISA 2000–2022 country notes for Finland · Basic Education Act (Finland), on fees in private schools. Text written for this course.

25.title: The rise and fall of the handshake
25.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Where the handshake came from, and what is happening to it now.

Before you read: the handshake is about five hundred years old in Europe. Why do you think it started?

Choose one. The text gives one popular answer — see if it is yours.

1 · Read the text once. Match a heading to each paragraph.

One minute. Do not write anything else yet.

The rise and fall of the handshake

A  Nobody knows exactly when people started to shake hands. One popular idea is that an open hand showed you carried no weapon, so the handshake began as a sign of trust and respect. For hundreds of years it was the safest greeting in business: firm, short, the same for everyone.

B  Then, in 2020, the world stopped touching. Doctors explained that a single handshake can move germs from one palm to another in a second, and that a virus travels fastest between people who greet each other all day. Offices put up notices: you must wash your hands, and you don’t have to shake hands with anyone.

C  Five years later, the handshake has not disappeared, but it now shares the job with other greetings. In many places a nod, a smile or a fist bump has taken its place. Some people think this trend is ridiculous. Others say it is simply more informal — and more honest.

D  So what happens next? If the flu season is bad, offices will go back to the elbow bump. If you meet a client in Germany, you will probably still shake hands. If you get it wrong, nobody will be angry — but the first impression might be strange. And if you are not sure what to do, watch the other person’s hand: if it comes forward, take it.

E  Perhaps the real rule is older than the handshake. If you greet people warmly, they will remember you. The hand is only the messenger.

Sources. Written for this course from public-health reporting on greetings and hand hygiene from 2020 onwards, and from the standard account of the handshake as a gesture that showed an empty hand. The offices, the notices and the individual examples are invented.

28.title: A question of taste
28.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Why two people can eat the same thing and disagree completely.

Before you read: some people love very bitter food and some cannot swallow it.

What do you think the main reason is? Choose one, then read and find out.

No right answer yet. This is your prediction.

A question of taste

Written for this course · A2

Two people sit down to the same plate of food. One eats happily; the other cannot finish it. Scientists now think that liking or disliking a food is not one thing but three.

What you are born with. Your tongue is covered with taste buds, and people do not have the same number of them. Researchers at the Monell Chemical Senses Center describe a group they call “supertasters”: roughly a quarter of people, who have far more taste buds than average. For them a plain green vegetable is not plain at all — it is strongly bitter, and a very sour or spicy dish can be painful. Avoiding spinach, then, is not fussiness. It is information.

What you grow up with. Babies already know the flavours their mother ate, because those flavours reach them before birth. After that, the rule is simple: the more often a child meets a food, the more likely they are to accept it. Studies suggest it takes eight to ten tastes, not one: a herb or a spice that is strange at four is ordinary at six. Giving up after the second refusal is the mistake most parents make.

What it feels like. Texture decides more than people admit. Many children who happily eat a boiled carrot will refuse the same carrot raw, and many adults who like the flavour of an olive still cannot eat one. It is not the taste. It is the mouth.

So the next time somebody leaves something on the plate, the answer is probably not that they are being polite about your cooking.

Sources. Taste-bud variation and the supertaster group: Monell Chemical Senses Center · flavour learning before birth and repeated exposure: published infant-feeding research summarised by the British Nutrition Foundation · texture and food refusal: BBC Future. Written for this course; no source text is reproduced.

31.title: If I ran the world
31.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

The year the United Nations asked the world what to fix first.

Before you read: the UN asked people in almost every country to choose the six things that would make the most difference to their lives. What do you think came first?

A prediction, not an answer. The text tells you in paragraph two.

One question, seven million answers

Before the United Nations agreed its development goals for 2030, it did something unusual: it asked the world what to put in them. The survey was called MY World. It gave people a list of sixteen issues, from a good education to action on climate change, and asked one question: if you could choose only six, which six would make the most difference to your life? By the end of 2014 more than seven million people, on every continent, had voted; most of them voted on paper. It is still one of the largest surveys ever carried out.

The answer was not the one many people in Europe expected. First came a good education. Then better healthcare, and then better job opportunities. An honest and responsive government was high on the list in every region. Affordable food — the hunger question — sat in the middle. Political freedoms, reliable energy at home, and phone and internet access came near the bottom — and so did action on climate change.

That last result needs care. It does not mean that the world thinks global warming is not an issue. When the researchers looked at rich and poor countries separately, they found a clear financial pattern: the richer the country, the higher climate action was placed. If you had secure work, clean water and a school for your children, you would have room to think about the coral reef and the natural disaster. If you did not, you would choose the school.

A list like this is powerful because nobody chose it for the voters. If the survey ran again today, the order might change, but the top probably would not. And if you could change one thing about the world, what would it be?

Sources. UN MY World survey, run by UNDP, the UN Millennium Campaign, the Overseas Development Institute and the World Wide Web Foundation; results published 2013–2015. From those published results: the list of sixteen issues and the choice of six; the top three priorities; the position of climate action, political freedoms and internet access at the bottom; the vote total by the end of 2014; and the finding that the priority given to climate action rises with a country’s level of development. Written for this course; no wording is taken from the reports.

32.title: The way things used to be
32.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

How long the news used to take, and what changed.

Before you read: two hundred years ago, how long did news take to travel from one town to the next?

Decide first. The answer is in the first paragraph.

How the news used to travel

Two hundred years ago, news moved at the speed of a horse. A robbery in one town used to take three days to reach the next. People used to read a weekly paper, not a daily one, and by the time an article about a flood or a forest fire arrived, the water had gone down and the fire was out. Nobody expected anything else.

Then came the telegraph. From the 1840s, messages ran along wires almost as fast as light. A hurricane in one country could be reported in another the same afternoon. Newspapers that used to appear once a week began to appear every morning, and the men who set up those first daily papers became rich. Editors who used to wait weeks for the post now waited minutes for the wire.

Today a crash, a strike or an election result reaches a phone in seconds. That is not only good news. When a volcano erupts we find out at once — but we also find out about a thousand things that will never matter to us. People who grew up before the internet often say the same thing: they used to know less, but they used to feel calmer. If you could choose, would you go back?

One detail is easy to miss. The telegraph did not only make the news faster; it made it shorter. Sending a message cost money by the word, so reporters learned to cut everything that was not necessary. The short, flat sentence of modern news writing was invented by people trying to save a few coins.

Sources. Written for this course from published media history: T. Standage, The Victorian Internet · Reuters Institute, Digital News Report. Dates are approximate.

34.title: The world of work
34.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

How long people really stay in the job they have.

Before you read: in the UK, how long does the average worker stay with one employer?

Choose one, then read and find out if you were right.

There is no right answer to guess. Guessing just makes you look for the number.

The people who stay, and the people who move

Fifty years ago, most people chose one profession and stayed in it. Their parents had done the same. A man who started work on a building site at eighteen often left the same company at sixty-five. People used to talk about “a job for life”, and they meant it.

Today the picture is different. In the United Kingdom the average worker stays with one employer for about five years. Some professions hold on to their staff for much longer. Judges have worked in the same court for twenty or thirty years. Nurses stay in health care even when they move hospital: one survey found that a nurse has usually worked in the profession for eleven years before she thinks about leaving it. In construction and in sales the numbers are much lower, and many people move on after two or three years.

Money is not the whole answer. Ana Ruiz has worked in the same laboratory since 2011. “I could earn more somewhere else,” she says, “but I have known these people for fourteen years.” Tom Baker, an accountant, moved four times in six years. “I used to think that was normal,” he says. “Now I have been with this business for eight years and I don’t want to move again. The clients know me. The office is open-plan and noisy, but the staff are good. That matters more than I thought it would.”

There is one more thing the numbers do not show. People who stay a long time are often the ones who changed something inside the job — a new team, a new zone of the building, a different day-to-day routine — instead of changing the job itself.

Sources. Written for this course from public labour-market data: UK Office for National Statistics, job tenure series · NHS Digital, workforce statistics · OECD, Employment by job tenure intervals. Figures are rounded. Ana Ruiz and Tom Baker are composites written for this course; no words are attributed to a real person.

35.title: The changing face of work
35.html:
Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

What changed when the office stopped being the place.

Before you read: when a team stops sharing an office, what happens to the amount of paperwork?

Decide first. The text answers this in paragraph two.

What a job involves now

Ten years ago almost nobody in Europe worked from home. Then, very quickly, millions of people had to. Today about one worker in four in the European Union is remote or hybrid — at home for part of the week, in the office for the rest. Some companies have worked this way for five years now and say they will not go back. Companies that used to measure a working day in hours try to measure it in results instead.

The job titles have not changed much, but the day-to-day work has. A manager’s first task used to be to watch the room. Now it is to write things down. “My job is to make the work visible,” says Priya Menon, who has led a hybrid team in Bengaluru since 2020. “If nobody can see you, somebody has to explain in detail what everyone is doing.” That means more paperwork, not less: reports, notes, and a short written answer to every enquiry.

Not everything is better. It is harder to train a new candidate when the team is in five places. Managers say it takes longer to recruit, and much longer to know whether the new person is any good. But productivity has not fallen. In most studies it has stayed the same or risen slightly, and workers say the same three things: they are less often in a hurry, their week is more flexible, and they are no longer in trouble for arriving ten minutes late.

One warning sits under all of this. The people who do best in a hybrid team already knew everybody before the team split up. For a new candidate, the first six months are much harder than they used to be, and no amount of paperwork fixes that.

Sources. Written for this course from public research: Eurofound, Living and working in the EU (telework series) · Eurostat, employed persons working from home · Bloom, Han & Liang (2024), Nature 630, on hybrid work and productivity. Figures are rounded. Priya Menon is a composite manager written for this course; no words are attributed to a real person.
